speaker_role: student (recent applicant sharing personal interview experience, not an admissions officer)
key_insights: Interviewed in person or remotely for 8+ schools (Harvard twice, Stanford, Yale, Princeton, Dartmouth, Vanderbilt, Tufts, Hamilton, plus Cornell and UPenn); was admitted to nearly all, waitlisted at Cornell, and rejected at Princeton, suggesting interview performance alone doesn't determine outcomes
Not all schools offer interviews; some require opting in on the application/portal while others assign one automatically, so applicants should check individually
Recommends quiet coffee shops or public libraries as interview locations, and 'casual but nice' dress (avoiding both suits and hoodies/sweats)
Categorizes interview styles into three types: interviewer-driven Q&A, natural back-and-forth conversation, or interviewer mostly sharing their own experience with the applicant asking questions
Recommends preparing two to three flexible 'go-to' stories that can be adapted to answer many different possible questions, refined across less-important interviews first
Suggests researching the interviewer in advance via LinkedIn/Google to find shared interests or relevant topics to raise early in the conversation
Recommends scheduling interviews at lower-priority schools first as practice runs before higher-priority school interviews
Advises sending a follow-up thank-you email referencing something specific discussed in the interview
specific_numbers_or_facts: Lists 10+ actual interview questions received across schools (e.g., 'tell me about yourself,' 'why this major,' 'biggest challenge you've faced') based on personal experience
notable_or_distinctive: Provides a concrete compiled list of real interview questions across many top schools from personal experience, plus the tactical tip of deliberately scheduling lower-priority interviews first as practice.
reliability_notes: Single student's anecdotal, largely successful outcome (admitted almost everywhere), so advice may not generalize; speaker explicitly states she is not an expert; transcript is relatively clean.
